open_points.subject: confirmation-time import conflicts
open_points.text:
rule 6, restated 2026-11-24: the mapping the step
showed, so a clean step's confirmation finds no new conflict
open_points.question: Must this passage be removed and replaced with the accepted guarantee that the mapping rebuilt in the confirming transaction may find a newly created id conflict and then refuses the import as `mapping_not_clean`?
options: Allow a new conflict at confirmation and refuse the whole import as `mapping_not_clean`.
Guarantee that a clean step can never acquire a new conflict before confirmation.
open_points.default_guess: Allow a new conflict at confirmation and refuse the whole import, matching the later A16 rule 6 restatement.

witness.initial: A clean import mapping and confirmation step have been shown; the import remains open.
events: After the step is shown, Registry mints for an ordinary create an id equal to an id in the picks.
The owner submits the bound import confirmation.
`confirm_import` rebuilds the mapping inside its transaction.
outcomes: The quoted State 5 passage says the clean step's confirmation finds no new conflict and can apply.
A16 rule 6 says the rebuilt mapping finds the conflict, refuses the whole import and changes nothing.
witness.observer: The owner sees either an accepted import or a `mapping_not_clean` refusal; the store either gains the imported records or remains unchanged.

open_points.subject: owner-session cookie attributes
open_points.text:
On sign-in, the session cookie set: not readable by scripts, only to
the owner interface's own host name (A13 rule 1, 2026-11-25), always
HTTPS-only (A13 rule 1; owner, 2026-11-17), and never sent with a request another site started (`SameSite=Strict`; owner,
2026-11-24).
open_points.question: Must the public effect state the complete accepted cookie contract—cookie name from `OWNER_SESSION_COOKIE_NAME`, exactly `Secure`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/`, no `Domain`, and no other attributes—rather than leaving `Path` and the exact attribute set for later code to guess?
options: State the complete imported cookie-name and attribute guarantee in this operation.
State only the security-related attributes here and let State 6 infer the remaining attributes from the constant.
open_points.default_guess: State the complete guarantee because browser-visible cookie scope is an already accepted boundary effect.

witness.initial: The owner signs in at a route below `/sign-in`.
events: The interface sends the session cookie.
The owner later follows a form at another owner-interface path.
outcomes: With the required `Path=/`, the browser sends the cookie and the request reaches the existing session.
With an omitted Path left to a default, the browser may scope the cookie to the sign-in path and the later request is treated as having no session.
witness.observer: The owner and the owner interface.

open_points.subject: dedicated owner-interface host name
open_points.text: providing it and keeping every other HTTPS service of the host off it is a deployment step, carried to the deployment's owner (the Factory's platform deployment).
open_points.question: Which concrete host name, certificate and routing arrangement will give the owner interface a host-only cookie scope shared with no other HTTPS service?
options: Allocate a dedicated DNS host name and certificate terminating directly at the owner-interface route.
Allocate a dedicated internal/VPN host name and certificate reachable only through the owner's VPN.
Use a gateway with a dedicated host name whose virtual host forwards only to the owner interface.
consequences: A public or private DNS name needs lifecycle and certificate management but gives straightforward host isolation.
An internal/VPN name narrows reachability but requires every owner device to resolve and trust it.
A gateway centralizes TLS but must ensure no other service is routed under that host name.
open_points.requirement: the deployment gives the owner interface a host name of its own, under which no other HTTPS service answers
open_points.default_guess: Use a dedicated VPN-resolved host name and certificate routed only to the owner interface.

open_points.subject: test-release class-table mutation
open_points.text:
The check is made on every answer all the same, and it is shown
on a test release whose class tables — the imported
`SERVICE_HIGHEST_CLASSES` constant and the imported
`PERSONAL_DATA_FIELDS` constant (SPEC_STANDARD §15.3.1) — differ from the
first release's in the one row a test gives
open_points.question: Which exact service, reachable answer and single altered table row will each class-enforcement test use?
options: Lower one service's highest class below an answer it already reaches.
Add one reachable Kernel answer field to `PERSONAL_DATA_FIELDS`.
Generate separate one-row variants for the highest-class and personal-field tests.
consequences: Lowering a highest class exercises the general whole-answer refusal path.
Changing `PERSONAL_DATA_FIELDS` directly exercises Kernel's non-disclosure boundary.
Separate variants avoid changing two policy dimensions in one witness but require two generated test releases.
open_points.requirement: An answer that would carry a class above the token's highest is refused whole; Registry never answers part of it.
open_points.default_guess: Generate two one-row test-release variants: one lowering a service's highest class and one classifying a Kernel-reachable field as personal data.

open_points.subject: serialization of agent calls with session changes
open_points.text:
checked by the
Factory on the code that implements them; it is carried to Factory
verification
open_points.question: How will Factory verification prove that every agent-authority read and write takes the same write lock and checks its session inside that transaction?
options: Use an instrumented store backend with transaction barriers to force both commit orders.
Inspect the generated call graph and transaction mode for every agent-authority operation.
Combine structural inspection with one representative controlled race.
consequences: Barrier tests directly witness both histories but require a test-only synchronization facility.
Structural inspection covers every operation but proves shape rather than runtime lock behavior.
The combined approach gives broad coverage and a runtime witness at higher test complexity.
open_points.requirement: A call and every change of its session — a revocation, an archiving, the session's end — are applied one at a time
open_points.default_guess: Combine a generated call-graph check for all agent operations with one barrier-controlled race.

open_points.subject: constant-time comparison and random secret generation checks
open_points.text:
it is checked on
the code, where State 5 routes every such comparison through
`random_values.equal_in_constant_time` and makes every such value in
`random_values.make_secret_value` alone, and carried to Factory
verification
open_points.question: How will Factory verification establish that every secret comparison and every owner-session secret uses only the required providers?
options: Check the generated call graph for forbidden comparison and randomness paths.
Replace the random and comparison providers with recording test doubles and exercise every caller.
Use both a structural check and provider-spy tests.
consequences: A call-graph check covers unexecuted branches but depends on accurate static analysis.
Provider spies show runtime routing but only for exercised paths.
Using both detects structural bypasses and verifies actual calls at greater maintenance cost.
open_points.requirement: each is compared in constant time and never appears in a URL, a log line, a diagnostic or an audit entry
open_points.default_guess: Use both structural checks and recording test doubles.

open_points.subject: confirmation-time minted-id collision witness
open_points.text:
Through Registry's surfaces alone a minted id cannot be chosen, so the
refusal is checked on the code by the Factory — `confirm_import`
builds the mapping inside the confirming transaction and applies it
only when clean — and carried to Factory verification
open_points.question: How will Factory verification force and observe the otherwise improbable id collision between a shown import step and its confirmation?
options: Replace the random source so an intervening ordinary create mints an id from the import picks.
Seed the store directly with the conflicting id between the step and confirmation.
Use structural inspection only to verify rebuilding and the clean-mapping guard.
consequences: Replacing randomness follows the admissible product history and exercises the public workflow.
Direct store seeding is simpler but bypasses the stated only production path for the new id.
Structural inspection covers the guard but supplies no runtime refusal witness.
open_points.requirement: A confirmation whose mapping, built in the confirming transaction, is not clean is refused whole and nothing changes
open_points.default_guess: Replace the random source and create the conflicting production record through the ordinary operation.

open_points.subject: failed removal of a newly created store
open_points.text:
A removal that fails,
leaving an empty store of the release's version, cannot be made to happen
through the surfaces without failing the store's making too; it is
carried to Factory verification.
open_points.question: How will Factory verification induce a removal failure after successful store creation and listener failure without also preventing creation?
options: Use a filesystem fault injector that fails the selected close or removal call only.
Use a fake filesystem backend with a scripted operation sequence.
Verify the cleanup branch structurally without executing it.
consequences: Targeted fault injection closely models the real boundary but is platform-sensitive.
A fake filesystem is deterministic but tests the adapter as well as the policy.
Structural verification avoids platform dependence but gives no runtime artifact witness.
open_points.requirement: a start whose listener cannot be opened => it serves nothing, leaves no listener of it open, and the store holds the records it held before that start — for a store that start made new, no store, or, when its removal fails, an empty one holding no record but its audit sequence at 0
open_points.default_guess: Use a scripted filesystem adapter that permits creation and then fails the exact cleanup removal.

open_points.subject: interruption before new-store rename
open_points.text:
the interruption
itself needs a capability the surfaces do not have, and is carried to
Factory verification.
open_points.question: How will Factory verification stop store creation after the temporary file exists but before its rename?
options: Add a test-only barrier at the persistence backend's pre-rename boundary.
Use process termination triggered by a filesystem-operation wrapper.
Verify the rename ordering structurally and start from a prepared temporary file for the recovery test.
consequences: A barrier gives deterministic timing but introduces a test hook.
Process termination is realistic but slower and more platform-dependent.
Prepared state tests recovery but not that production code can leave only that state when interrupted.
open_points.requirement: at every start it first removes a file of that temporary name, left by an interrupted start, and no other file there
open_points.default_guess: Use a backend-level pre-rename barrier and terminate the test process there.

open_points.subject: backup snapshot instant ordering
open_points.text:
an implementation taking a backup's instant later than
the read that fixes its snapshot (rule 1) is not told apart; that remains
carried to Factory verification.
open_points.question: How will Factory verification distinguish an instant read at the snapshot-fixing audit-counter read from one read later?
options: Use a clock double that advances between the snapshot-fixing read and the next operation.
Instrument the store backend to record the order of the clock call and first database read.
Use a structural call-order check on `copy_store_snapshot`.
consequences: An advancing clock produces an observable wrong timestamp if ordering is incorrect.
Operation tracing proves runtime order without depending on timestamp values.
Structural inspection is broad but may miss backend behavior that reorders the actual read.
open_points.requirement: the instant being that of the read that fixes its snapshot
open_points.default_guess: Use an advancing clock double plus operation tracing around the first database read.

open_points.subject: overlapping pointer-publication serialization witness
open_points.text:
a deterministic witness would need a point to
hold a transaction, which the specification does not name, and remains
carried to Factory verification.
open_points.question: How will Factory verification make two publish transactions overlap deterministically?
options: Provide a test-only transaction barrier after the first publish takes the write lock.
Instrument the store backend to pause the first transaction at its first pointer read.
Rely on repeated probabilistic concurrency tests without a barrier.
consequences: A lock barrier deterministically proves serialization but adds test infrastructure.
A backend pause gives precise overlap while coupling the test to persistence operations.
Probabilistic tests require no hook but can pass without exercising the intended overlap.
open_points.requirement: Every publish and every withdrawal on one project's pointers is serialised with the others
open_points.default_guess: Use a test-store transaction barrier after the first caller acquires the write lock.

open_points.subject: concurrent create request-id witness
open_points.text:
a deterministic witness would need a point to hold a
transaction, which the specification does not name; that remains carried
to Factory verification.
open_points.question: How will Factory verification force concurrent creates with the same request id to overlap?
options: Pause the first transaction after its request-id lookup and before insert.
Pause the first transaction immediately after it acquires the write lock.
Run repeated unsynchronized concurrent calls.
consequences: Pausing after lookup targets the check-create race directly but exposes a persistence-level hook.
Pausing at lock acquisition proves serialization while remaining independent of record layout.
Repeated calls are simpler but do not guarantee the race was exercised.
open_points.requirement: of two concurrent creates, the first makes the record and the second is a repeat or refused by rule 4 or 5
open_points.default_guess: Pause the first transaction immediately after it acquires the write lock.

open_points.subject: unwitnessed A04 stage-order pairs
open_points.text:
the other pairs remain carried to Factory
verification.
open_points.question: How will Factory verification cover every applicable ordering pair not exercised by the named surface tests?
options: Generate a matrix of actions with two simultaneous failures for every applicable stage pair.
Inspect each generated operation pipeline against a canonical stage-order model.
Combine representative two-failure tests with a structural pipeline check.
consequences: A generated matrix gives behavioral evidence but can become large and action-specific.
Structural comparison covers all operations compactly but relies on accurate operation metadata.
The combined approach limits behavioral cases while still checking every generated pipeline.
open_points.requirement: Every operation — read or change, of a service, Kernel or the owner — checks in one order, and the first failure is its answer
open_points.default_guess: Use a structural pipeline check for every operation plus representative behavioral tests for each adjacent stage pair.

set_aside.subject: withdrawal contract in the derived manifest
set_aside.text:
### Inputs

The transaction; the pointer id; the withdrawing principal; the action's
instant.
set_aside.question: How must the derived manifest state that withdrawal has no idempotency-key input, is a `state-transition`, and refuses a replay, as R0-99 requires?
options: Omit the idempotency-key field and use an explicit replay-behavior value for refusal.
Represent the idempotency-key field as null and describe the refusal in the failure contract.
Represent replay refusal solely as a typed operation failure, with no separate replay field.
Use a shared write schema that forbids the idempotency field for withdrawal and declares an already-withdrawn failure.
consequences: An explicit replay value gives Kernel a direct machine-readable guarantee but requires that value in the manifest vocabulary.
A null field preserves a uniform shape but creates a distinct null-versus-omitted contract state.
A failure-only representation requires consumers to derive replay semantics from the failure contract.
A shared schema reduces variation but needs an exact forbidden-field rule.
set_aside.default_guess: Omit the idempotency-key field, declare effect class `state-transition`, and declare explicit replay behavior `repeat_refused`.

witness.initial: Kernel is generating a binding from Registry's derived manifest for `withdraw_pointer`.
events: The manifest generator reaches the withdrawal operation.
It must encode the operation's idempotency and replay contract without a State 5 decision fixing the representation.
outcomes: One generator omits the idempotency field and emits an explicit replay-refusal value.
Another emits a null idempotency field or only an already-withdrawn failure.
witness.observer: Kernel's binding and approval machinery, which receives different machine-readable contracts.
